findings.title: Pin and verify the remote script before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: The build executes mutable content fetched from an external URL as root. A compromised or changed endpoint, or a redirect, can run arbitrary commands in the image build and release environment.

findings.title: Fail the build when fetching the install script fails
findings.whyItBreaks: Without `--fail` or `pipefail`, curl's error can be discarded because the pipeline reports the final `sh` status. A connection failure can therefore produce a successful RUN layer without performing the install.

findings.title: Vendor or pin the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: The build downloads an unpinned HTTPS response and pipes it directly to Alpine's root shell. A compromised endpoint or redirect can execute arbitrary commands in the builder, alter the image, or exfiltrate build credentials.

findings.title: Pin and verify the script before executing it as root
findings.whyItBreaks: The image build executes whatever content the mutable remote URL serves with root privileges. A compromised endpoint, redirect target, or changed script can execute arbitrary commands and modify the resulting image.

findings.title: Propagate install-script download failures out of the build
findings.whyItBreaks: The pipeline reports the final sh status, not curl's status. A DNS, TLS, or connection failure can leave sh with empty input and return success, producing an image that appears successfully built without running the installation.

findings.title: Preserve the error in the new public helper
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for absent keys, but this helper discards the error and returns "". A missing key is therefore indistinguishable from a present key containing an empty string, preventing callers from handling the failure safely.

findings.title: Do not discard Load errors in LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but the ignored error causes LoadOrDefault to return "", which is indistinguishable from a present key whose value is empty. This exported API forces callers to treat a failed load as a real value.

findings.title: Preserve ErrMissing in LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key produces ErrMissing at src/store.go:10, but this exported helper ignores the error and returns an empty string. That is indistinguishable from a present key whose stored value is legitimately empty.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning from Run
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation completed each channel send before returning. These detached goroutines let Run return while results are still pending, so callers can observe incomplete output or close results and trigger a panic from a later send.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning from Run
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously each send completed before Run returned. The new goroutines may still be sending after return; a caller that closes its channel immediately can trigger a send-on-closed-channel panic, while blocked sends can leak goroutines and leave results undelivered.

findings.title: Wait for worker sends before returning from Run
findings.whyItBreaks: Run now launches one goroutine per job and returns without joining them. Callers can observe fewer than len(jobs) results immediately after Run returns, or close results after Run returns while a worker is still sending, which panics.

findings.title: Preserve Log's existing function type
findings.whyItBreaks: Log changed from func(string) to func(string, ...string). Go treats variadic and non-variadic function types as distinct, so downstream code passing or storing logger.Log where func(string) is required no longer compiles.

findings.title: Honor the optional tag in Log output
findings.whyItBreaks: Log now accepts tags, but the body still executes println(message) only, so callers supplying tag context silently lose it.

findings.title: Restore both authorization checks for deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: The OR authorizes any non-admin in the record's tenant and any admin regardless of tenant, bypassing the previous requirement that both conditions hold.

findings.title: Preserve tenant isolation for admin deletions
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing && to || makes canDeleteRecord return true whenever session.isAdmin is true, even when session.tenantId differs from record.tenantId. An admin from tenant A can therefore authorize deletion of tenant B's records, enabling cross-tenant data loss.

findings.title: Require both admin and tenant match before deleting
findings.whyItBreaks: The OR makes either condition sufficient: a non-admin in the record's tenant can delete it, and an admin from another tenant can delete across tenants.

findings.title: Preserve errors from invalid settings instead of saving defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: JSON parse and schema-validation failures previously propagated from lines 9-11. They now return defaults, so updateFontSize at line 20 treats invalid input as valid, changes the font size, and saves a replacement object at line 22, potentially discarding the user's theme or all recoverable settings.

findings.title: Preserve parse errors instead of persisting default settings
findings.whyItBreaks: parseSettings now converts JSON and validation errors into DEFAULTS. updateFontSize then changes the font size and calls save, so input such as {"theme":"dark"} is silently saved as {"theme":"light","fontSize":size}; before this change the error propagated and save was not called.

findings.title: Preserve parse errors before updateFontSize persists defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, JSON and schema errors propagated from parseSettings, so updateFontSize did not save. Now updateFontSize receives DEFAULTS, applies the requested size, and saves them, silently replacing settings such as a valid dark theme when other input is malformed.

findings.title: Use the selected commit for artifact lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: When the requested branch differs from the verified ref, builtFrom identifies the branch commit but artifactsAt loads artifacts from a different commit, producing an incorrect build report.

findings.title: Use the selected commit when loading artifacts
findings.whyItBreaks: When the requested branch and verified ref resolve to different commits, the report claims builtFrom is the branch commit but returns artifacts from verified, producing an internally inconsistent build report.

findings.title: Read artifacts from the requested commit
findings.whyItBreaks: buildFrom is resolved from the requested branch, but artifacts are resolved from build.ref("verified"). Whenever those refs differ, the report contains artifacts for a different commit; if the verified ref is absent, report generation fails.

findings.title: Return only the requested number of recent entries
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit, this returns the full reversed input instead of at most limit entries. renderFeed passes 20 at src/feed.ts:9 and its loop expands the nominal 20-element output to page.length at src/feed.ts:11.

findings.title: Apply the limit before returning recent entries
findings.whyItBreaks: For any limit greater than zero, recentEntries returns the entire reversed array. renderFeed passes 20 and then writes every returned entry, expanding its 20-slot result when more than 20 entries exist.

findings.title: Preserve the requested entry limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit, recentEntries now returns the entire reversed input instead of at most limit entries. renderFeed calls it with 20 and then copies every returned entry, so inputs with more than 20 entries produce an oversized feed.

findings.title: Count only live entries in the manifest header
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry is stale, the emitted rows contain only live entries but line 22 declares entries.length, producing a manifest whose entry-count exceeds its records. Consumers that trust the count can reject the manifest or read past its end.

findings.title: Count only live entries in the manifest header
findings.whyItBreaks: With one stale and one live entry, the output declares entry-count: 2 but emits only one row, producing an internally inconsistent manifest.

findings.title: Pass the filtered count to the manifest header
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry is stale, the output contains fewer rows than the `entry-count` header because line 22 still passes `entries.length` instead of the filtered count. Consumers can reject or misparse the manifest.

findings.title: Preserve the exported legacy ID formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: FormatLegacyID is an exported package symbol in the base revision. Removing it causes any downstream package that calls ids.FormatLegacyID to fail compilation on upgrade, even though there are no repository-local callers.

findings.title: Preserve the exported FormatLegacyID API
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported FormatLegacyID symbol is removed, so downstream packages importing example.com/app/ids and calling it now fail to compile with an undefined symbol.

findings.title: Preserve the existing shippingQuote export
findings.whyItBreaks: The base module exported shippingQuote, but this change only imports quoteShipping internally and does not re-export the old name. Existing TypeScript or ES module consumers importing shippingQuote from ./orders will fail after upgrading.

findings.title: Restore execute's successful return path
findings.whyItBreaks: Every invocation now throws Error("always fails"), so callers receive no string and the prior uppercase behavior is completely regressed.

findings.title: Restore execute's successful return path
findings.whyItBreaks: Every valid invocation now throws Error("always fails") and never returns the declared string result; the base implementation returned input.toUpperCase().

findings.title: Preserve execute's successful string result
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to execute now throws Error("always fails") synchronously, so no input produces the string result previously returned by the exported API.

findings.title: Preserve the active viewer read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: For an active viewer with fewer than five attempts, this new guard makes isEligible return false, so handle returns "rejected" at line 24 instead of reaching its existing "read-only" branch at line 25.

findings.title: Preserve the viewer read-only handling path
findings.whyItBreaks: handle() calls isEligible() at line 24. For an active viewer with fewer than five attempts, this new guard returns false, so handle() returns "rejected" instead of the existing "read-only" result at line 25. This makes the viewer read-only action unreachable.

findings.title: Keep viewers eligible for the existing read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: For an active viewer with fewer than five attempts, the new check makes isEligible return false, so handle returns "rejected" at line 24 and never reaches its existing "read-only" branch at line 25. The base behavior returned "read-only".

findings.title: Do not block draft saves on payment status
findings.whyItBreaks: saveDraft passes draft orders with payment="missing" through canProceed; the new condition returns false, so src/actions.ts:9 returns "blocked" instead of saving the draft. Payment should gate submission, not draft persistence.

findings.title: Keep unpaid drafts saveable
findings.whyItBreaks: saveDraft shares canProceed, so a draft with payment="missing" now fails the new condition and returns "blocked" instead of "saved". Saving a draft is distinct from submitting an order and should not require payment.

findings.title: Keep payment gating out of draft saves
findings.whyItBreaks: For an order with state=draft and payment=missing, canProceed now returns false, so saveDraft returns blocked instead of saved. The payment requirement should govern submission, not draft persistence.

findings.title: Read files from the requested channel commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The returned commit is headCommit(channel), but files are read from headCommit("stable"). When those refs differ, the snapshot metadata and file contents describe different commits.

findings.title: Read files from the requested channel head
findings.whyItBreaks: The snapshot commit comes from the requested channel, but files now come from the stable channel. When those heads differ, the snapshot exposes stable content under another channel's commit.

findings.title: Read files from the requested channel head
findings.whyItBreaks: When the requested channel head differs from stable, Snapshot.commit identifies the requested head but Snapshot.files contains stable's contents, producing an internally inconsistent published snapshot.

findings.title: Honor the new `limit` argument
findings.whyItBreaks: build(..., limit=3) still returns 10 items because max_count remains hard-coded to 10.

findings.title: Use `limit` instead of the hard-coded count
findings.whyItBreaks: The function accepts `limit`, but `max_count` remains hard-coded to 10 and drives the loop. A call such as `build("x", limit=3)` still returns 10 items, making the new public parameter ineffective.

findings.title: Use limit to determine the number of generated items
findings.whyItBreaks: Callers passing a limit receive 10 items regardless of the requested value because max_count remains hard-coded to 10.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The renamed helper promises a positive integer, but its body only calls int(value). charge at line 6 therefore accepts -1 or 0 and returns -100 or 0 cents.

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The renamed public function still accepts 0 and negative values, so charge() can produce zero or negative cents instead of rejecting invalid amounts.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int

findings.whyItBreaks: The assignment now writes directly into the caller-owned df, and return df returns that same object. The base implementation copied df first, so callers that reuse the original DataFrame now observe silently changed values.

findings.title: Keep the input dataframe immutable during value application
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation copied df before applying mappings. This line now writes directly into the caller's dataframe, so callers retaining or reusing the input observe unintended value changes and can suffer cross-operation contamination.

findings.title: Preserve the input DataFrame instead of mutating caller data
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation copied df before applying assignments. These lines now write directly into the caller's DataFrame, so any caller that reuses or retains the input unexpectedly observes the mapped values.

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: parse_positive_int("-5") returns -5 because parse() accepts signed integers, so charge("-5") returns -500. The public function name promises positive output, but callers receive a negative value.

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The public function name promises a positive integer, but its implementation returns parsed negatives unchanged. Consequently, charge("-1") produces -100 instead of enforcing the positive-input contract.

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The public name promises a positive integer, but the body accepts negatives and returns 0 for invalid input. Consequently, charge("-1") returns -100 through the changed call site.

findings.whyItBreaks: When the pinned tag resolves to A and latest resolves to B, the changeset contains fromRevision=A but paths computed from B. Consumers replaying those paths on A can apply an incorrect or incomplete change set.

When those revisions differ, the path list does not describe the base revision consumers replay the changeset on, causing changes to be omitted or misapplied.

findings.title: Update the query for the renamed column

findings.title: Update the query when renaming users.email

findings.whyItBreaks: Every client now receives the committed live key instead of the deployment's BILLING_API_KEY. Anyone with repository or build access can use the credential, and rotating or isolating credentials per environment no longer works.

findings.title: Restore environment-based billing credentials
findings.whyItBreaks: The tracked source now contains a live billing credential, allowing repository readers to reuse it. Every deployment also uses this same credential, including deployments with a missing or different BILLING_API_KEY; the previous fail-fast configuration error is gone.

findings.title: Remove the hardcoded live billing credential
findings.whyItBreaks: The source now exposes a bk_live credential and every environment uses it, ignoring BILLING_API_KEY. Anyone with the repository can reuse the credential, and deployments can bill through the wrong account.

findings.whyItBreaks: When gw.Submit returns an error, this branch only logs it and Charge returns nil at line 19. Callers therefore observe success after a declined or failed gateway submission and may record or act on an unpaid charge.

findings.title: Propagate gateway failures from Charge
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, gw.Submit errors were wrapped and returned. This line now only logs the error, while line 19 unconditionally returns nil, forcing callers to treat failed charges as successful.

findings.title: Include tenantId in cacheKey
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A caches a setting under settings:name, tenant B hits the same entry and receives A's value without calling its own SettingsStore.fetch. This breaks tenant isolation and returns incorrect configuration.

findings.title: Keep tenant identity in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: The module-level cache is now keyed only by name. After tenant A loads a setting, tenant B requesting the same name receives A's value without calling its own store, causing cross-tenant disclosure and incorrect configuration.

findings.title: Preserve the two-argument invalidation API
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported API previously accepted invalidate(tenantId, name). Existing JavaScript callers now bind tenantId as name and delete settings:<tenantId> instead of the requested entry; TypeScript callers fail on the changed arity, leaving cached settings stale.

findings.title: Keep tenant identity in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: store.fetch remains tenant-scoped at src/settings.ts:15, but the cache key now uses only name. Once tenant A caches a setting, tenant B requesting the same name receives A's value without calling its own store, causing cross-tenant data disclosure or misconfiguration.

findings.title: Serialize concurrent reservations per SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: The await leaves stock at the old count. Two overlapping reserve calls can both pass the guard, save the same decremented value, and return true for one available unit.

findings.title: Serialize concurrent reservations per SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: With stock=1, two concurrent calls both read remaining=1 before either save resolves, both persist 0, and both return true. One inventory unit is therefore reserved twice.

findings.title: Serialize concurrent reservations for the same SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: The await yields after reading the current count but before decrementing the map. With one item, two concurrent calls both read 1, both persist 0, and both resolve true, allowing two reservations for one item.

findings.title: Preserve or version the exported Inventory API
findings.whyItBreaks: The base API had an implicit no-argument constructor and synchronous reserve(): boolean. Existing consumers using new Inventory() can now fail when reserve reaches this.store.save, while callers using if (inventory.reserve(sku)) now test a truthy Promise instead of the reservation result.

findings.title: Remove the extra retry delay conversion
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds, but retry() still calls sleep(backoff(a) * 1000). The first retry waits 1,000,000 ms instead of 1,000 ms, and capped retries wait 30,000,000 ms instead of 30,000 ms.

findings.title: Remove the extra millisecond conversion from retry delays
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1000 milliseconds, but retry still multiplies it by 1000 at src/jobs/retry.ts:12, causing the first retry to wait 1,000,000 ms (16.7 minutes) instead of 1 second and the cap to become 30,000,000 ms (8.3 hours).

findings.title: Keep retry delays in the same unit as backoff
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds, but retry() still multiplies the result by 1000 at src/jobs/retry.ts:12. The first retry waits 1,000,000 ms instead of 1,000 ms, and the cap becomes 30,000,000 ms instead of 30,000 ms.

findings.title: Return the file-close error from Save
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred f.Close() error is ignored. If Flush succeeds but Close reports a delayed I/O or filesystem error, Save returns nil and callers cannot detect that the write failed.

findings.title: Return file-close errors from Save
findings.whyItBreaks: If w.Flush succeeds but f.Close returns an error, the deferred call is ignored and Save returns nil, so callers cannot distinguish close failure from successful persistence.

findings.title: Return file-close errors from Save
findings.whyItBreaks: If w.Flush succeeds but f.Close returns an error, the deferred call discards it and Save returns nil, so callers cannot detect a failed or incomplete persistence operation.

findings.title: Include the upper-bound row in each page window
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns half-open [start, end) bounds, but range(start, end - 1) excludes the last valid position. A one-row page renders empty, and every larger page silently loses its final row through render_page and summarize.

findings.title: Iterate through the exclusive page end
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open end, but range(start, end - 1) excludes the final valid position. A two-row page visits only its first row, and a page_size of 1 returns no rows. render_page and summarize therefore silently lose data.

findings.title: Use the full half-open range for each page
findings.whyItBreaks: The bounds are half-open, but range(start, end - 1) excludes the final valid position. A one-row page returns no rows, and render_page/summarize emit incomplete output.

findings.title: Return fresh entries and evict expired cache entries
findings.whyItBreaks: For a newly stored entry, age is below ttlMs, so this condition deletes it and returns null. Once age exceeds ttlMs, it returns the expired value instead.

findings.title: Remove completed jobs without splicing during iteration
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing shifts the next element into the removed element's index while forEach advances, so adjacent completed jobs are skipped. For two consecutive done jobs, the second remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's jobs array while pruning
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation returned a new filtered array, but splice now mutates the caller-owned jobs array, unexpectedly removing entries from any retained queue reference.

findings.title: Restore the fresh-entry TTL check
findings.whyItBreaks: The inverted comparison deletes fresh entries and returns values after they have expired. With ttlMs=1000, age 0 returns null while age 1001 returns stale data.

findings.title: Avoid splicing jobs during forEach
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an element shifts later elements left while forEach advances its original index. For [done a, done b], a is removed and b is skipped, so a completed job remains; the input array is also newly mutated.

findings.title: Restore fresh-entry semantics in TtlCache.get
findings.whyItBreaks: With a normal positive TTL, fresh entries have age < ttlMs, so this branch deletes them and returns null. Expired entries have age > ttlMs, so it returns stale values instead.

findings.title: Use filtering to prune all completed jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing while forEach increments its index causes adjacent completed jobs to be skipped; for example, [done, done, pending] returns [done, pending]. This also mutates the caller's array, unlike the previous implementation.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input result in averageAmount
findings.whyItBreaks: With rows = [], total is 0 and rows.length is 0, so averageAmount now returns NaN. The base implementation explicitly returned 0.

findings.title: Avoid mutating the input array in busiest
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort mutates rows in place, so calling busiest changes the caller's array order. The base implementation sorted a defensive copy.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-average result
findings.whyItBreaks: averageAmount([]) now computes 0 / 0 and returns NaN; the base implementation explicitly returned 0, so empty datasets now produce a non-finite metric that can contaminate downstream calculations.

findings.title: Do not sort the caller's rows array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort mutates rows, so calling busiest changes the caller's row order. The base implementation sorted a copy and preserved the input array.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input average result
findings.whyItBreaks: averageAmount([]) now reduces to 0 and computes 0 / 0, returning NaN instead of the previous 0. Callers can no longer treat an empty result as a usable numeric zero.

findings.title: Do not sort the caller's rows array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: rows.sort(...) mutates the input array, so calling busiest(rows) permanently reorders caller-owned data by amount. The previous spread copy preserved the caller's ordering.

findings.title: Use numeric comparison when ranking scores
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() converts numbers to strings and sorts lexicographically. For scores 20, 100, and 3, rankScores returns [3, 20, 100], so topPlayers(..., 1) uses cutoff 3 and can return the first input player instead of the 100-score player.

findings.title: Use a numeric comparator for score ranking
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() orders numbers lexicographically. For scores [2, 10], reverse() yields [2, 10], so topPlayers(..., 1) sets the cutoff to 2 and can return the lower-scoring player based on input order.

findings.title: Keep leaderboard scores in numeric descending order
findings.whyItBreaks: sort() converts numbers to strings before comparing. For scores [9, 10], reverse() produces [9, 10], so topPlayers(..., 1) sets cutoff to 9 and can return the 9-point player instead of the 10-point player.

findings.title: Restore constant-time comparison for webhook signatures
findings.whyItBreaks: Python string equality can exit at the first mismatching character, exposing the expected HMAC prefix through response timing. An attacker can use the webhook endpoint as an oracle to forge a signature and reach processor(payload).

findings.title: Restore constant-time comparison for webhook signatures
findings.whyItBreaks: Ordinary string equality can short-circuit on the first mismatched character, exposing the expected HMAC prefix through timing measurements. An attacker can use this oracle to forge a signature and reach processor(payload) instead of receiving 401.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Ordinary string equality can return after the first mismatching character. Because given_signature is attacker-controlled and handle uses verify to authorize processor execution at app/webhook.py:14, repeated requests can expose the valid HMAC prefix through timing measurements and enable forged webhook requests.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction exits and commits the ledger insert at line 23 before _apply_balances runs. If either balance update fails, the ledger row remains committed while balances are unchanged or only partially updated.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction exits after inserting the ledger row at line 23, then balance updates run separately. A process failure or database error after the ledger commit can leave the ledger recorded without matching balance changes, or only the debit applied.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger insert is committed when the transaction context exits, before either balance update runs. If a balance update fails, the ledger entry remains while balances are unchanged or only the source balance is modified; concurrent readers can also observe the ledger without matching balances.

findings.title: Keep billing-day extraction in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation used UTC calendar fields, but this change uses local-time getters. For example, in America/Los_Angeles, 2024-01-02T00:30:00Z now produces 2024-01-01 instead of 2024-01-02; sameBillingDay inherits this regression.

findings.title: Keep billing-day extraction in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation used UTC getters, while this change uses host-local getters. For example, 2026-01-01T23:30:00Z becomes 2026-01-02 in Asia/Taipei, changing billing-day keys and sameBillingDay results based on deployment timezone.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when computing the billing day
findings.whyItBreaks: getFullYear/getMonth/getDate use the host timezone. For example, 2026-08-31T00:30:00Z becomes 2026-08-30 in America/Los_Angeles, whereas the previous implementation returned 2026-08-31. This changes billing grouping and sameBillingDay results near UTC midnight.

findings.title: Restore tenant isolation in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant-a/account-1 is cached, tenant-b/account-1 uses the same key and receives tenant-a's Profile from the module-global memo without calling fetchProfile. This returns incorrect cross-tenant data.

findings.title: Keep tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: Calls for the same account in different tenants now share one cache entry. After tenant A caches a profile, tenant B receives tenant A's profile without fetchProfile running, causing cross-tenant data exposure and incorrect profile data.

findings.title: Preserve tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: Calls for the same account in different tenants now share one cache entry. After tenant A is cached, tenant B receives tenant A's profile without calling fetchProfile, leaking and misidentifying profile data.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors from the public loader
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation propagated an error for a missing key, but the new catch-all returns "". Callers cannot distinguish a missing key from a valid empty-string value; loadAll now silently emits empty entries.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously propagated an Error, but the catch now returns "". This makes absent data indistinguishable from a valid empty value, and loadAll returns that fallback for missing keys.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported load function now catches the missing-key error and returns "". loadAll therefore returns an apparently valid value for missing entries, which is indistinguishable from a legitimately stored empty string.

findings.title: Expose exhaustion from retryBackground
findings.whyItBreaks: Every exception from fn is caught and discarded. After all retries or the deadline, the exported function returns void, making callback failure indistinguishable from success for callers.

findings.title: Preserve the existing timeoutMs Config field
findings.whyItBreaks: Config and retry are exported. Existing TypeScript callers using { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } no longer type-check because timeoutMs was removed and retries is now required. Untyped callers pass undefined to retry, making Date.now() + config.timeout NaN so the timeout guard never fires.

findings.title: Expose retryBackground's terminal failure
findings.whyItBreaks: Every exception from fn is discarded. When all attempts fail, retryBackground returns normally with void, indistinguishable from a successful callback, so callers cannot detect failed work.

findings.title: Propagate retryBackground callback failures
findings.whyItBreaks: Every exception from fn is caught and discarded. After the final retry, or when the deadline is reached, the exported void function returns normally, forcing callers to treat exhausted failure as success.

findings.title: Keep the supplied value as the input default
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation initialized the input with value; this now initializes every field with len=<length> (for example, abc becomes len=3), changing what users see, edit, and submit.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now publicly accepts number, but number has no length property, so TypeScript rejects this expression; if type checking is bypassed, a numeric value produces len=undefined.

findings.title: Preserve the supplied value as the input default
findings.whyItBreaks: A string value such as "abc" previously initialized the input to "abc", but now initializes it to "len=3". Numeric values produce "len=undefined" because numbers have no length, and TypeScript rejects the union property access.

findings.title: Handle numbers before accessing value.length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now permits numbers, but number has no length property, so TypeScript rejects this component; unchecked transpilation would produce len=undefined for numeric values.

findings.title: Preserve the supplied value in the input
findings.whyItBreaks: For the previously supported string input, defaultValue changes from the caller's value to len=<length>; for example, value="abc" renders len=3 instead of abc.

findings.title: Stop printing the deployment token in workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The step expands secrets.TOKEN and writes it to workflow stdout, creating a credential-disclosure path for log consumers.

findings.title: Do not print the deployment token in workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: When TOKEN is configured, this command expands and writes the deployment credential to stdout. GitHub masking is not a reliable security boundary for all secret values or log handling, so a log reader may recover and reuse the token.

findings.title: Retain the large-output buffer for git commands
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer makes spawnSync use Node's 1 MiB default. A valid PR whose git diff output at line 140 exceeds that limit is terminated/truncated, causing git() to throw before the try block at line 175; the adapter then aborts without posting the review or check. Node documents this default and behavior in the child_process API: https://nodejs.org/api/child_process.html.

findings.title: Restore the Git subprocess output limit
findings.whyItBreaks: The git diff at line 140 can exceed Node's default spawnSync stdout buffer. That returns ENOBUFS with a null status, causing git() to throw before the review and check are posted.

findings.title: Restore the buffer for large git diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: git() now uses spawnSync's default 1 MiB output limit instead of the previous 64 MiB limit. The git diff at line 140 can exceed that limit, causing the review setup to abort before review(bundle) runs.

findings.title: Preserve the read-only sandbox for review runs
findings.whyItBreaks: The wrapper previously forced every Codex invocation to use read-only mode. It now inherits sandbox_mode from user configuration; with workspace-write or danger-full-access configured, model-generated commands can modify or delete files in opts.repoPath, allowing prompt-injected review content to bypass the agent's read-only isolation.

findings.title: Keep review subprocesses in the read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: Without `-s read-only`, `codex exec` uses the configured sandbox policy. A user or project configured for `workspace-write` or `danger-full-access` can therefore cause an untrusted review prompt or repository content to modify files during a review, removing the wrapper's safety boundary. The CLI documents that `--sandbox/-s` controls model-generated commands and otherwise defaults to configuration ([official reference](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/developer-commands?surface=cli)).

findings.title: Keep review runs in a read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: Without `-s read-only`, `codex exec` inherits configuration/defaults; version-controlled projects can use workspace-write, which permits edits and command execution in `opts.repoPath`. A prompt injection in reviewed code can therefore mutate the checkout or compromise review integrity. Codex documents this behavior in its [sandbox security guidance](https://developers.openai.com/codex/agent-approvals-security).

findings.title: Use headSha as the diff endpoint
findings.whyItBreaks: PR_HEAD_SHA explicitly overrides headSha on line 137, but these calls hard-code HEAD. When the checkout is a merge ref or stale commit, the bundle reviews baseSha..HEAD while the review and check are posted for headSha, so PR changes can be omitted or unrelated checkout changes can be reviewed.

findings.title: Use the PR head and merge base for the review range
findings.whyItBreaks: headSha is explicitly sourced from PR_HEAD_SHA, but these commands ignore it and diff baseSha against local HEAD. When Actions checks out a synthetic pull-request merge commit, or when the base branch advanced after the PR branched, the review receives a different patch and changed-file set than the PR. It can miss PR changes, include base/merge-resolution changes, and produce findings that are posted against the unrelated headSha.

findings.title: Keep the merge-base diff so base changes stay out of reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: When the PR head F forked from B0 but PR_BASE_SHA is a newer base tip B1, `git diff B1 HEAD` computes the net base-to-head difference instead of the PR-only B0-to-F difference. It can review unrelated base changes or hide a PR change that B1 independently made, causing `review(bundle)` to analyze the wrong patch.

findings.title: Preserve literal prompt data during placeholder replacement
findings.whyItBreaks: String replacement interprets sequences such as $&, $$, $` and $' in bundle.patch instead of inserting them literally. A valid diff containing one of these sequences is therefore altered before runCodex receives it, producing an incorrect review prompt.

findings.title: Keep interpolated prompt content literal
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace treats the new string replacement as a template. Bundle content containing $&, $`, $', or $$ is rewritten before runCodex; for example, $& becomes the {{BUNDLE}} placeholder. The same regression affects candidate findings and patches at lines 32-33, causing Codex to review corrupted evidence.

findings.title: Preserve literal payloads in prompt replacements
findings.whyItBreaks: String replacement values interpret sequences such as $$, $&, $` and $'. A valid patch or finding containing one of these sequences is therefore altered when inserted into reviewPrompt or criticPrompt, potentially duplicating prompt text, dropping characters, or injecting the surrounding prompt into the payload before runCodex receives it. The same regression exists at lines 32-33.

findings.title: Keep the analyzed SHA in the fallback review request
findings.whyItBreaks: If the JSON request fails and the PR advances after headSha is captured, the fallback omits commit_id and GitHub associates the review with the PR's latest commit. The review body can therefore request changes against code that was never analyzed.

findings.title: Preserve the analyzed SHA in the fallback review request
findings.whyItBreaks: When the JSON review request fails, the fallback omits commit_id. GitHub then defaults the review to the pull request's most recent commit. If the PR advances during review, the verdict is posted for code that was not analyzed, while the check remains attached to the original headSha.

findings.title: Keep the analyzed commit in the fallback review
findings.whyItBreaks: The fallback no longer sends headSha. GitHub defaults an omitted commit_id to the pull request's latest commit ([API documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/pulls/reviews)); if the PR advances after headSha is captured, this submits findings generated for one commit against another, making the review stale or incorrectly associated.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating valid-looking records
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding({}) now returns severity P1, category bug, empty required strings, and lineStart/lineEnd 0 instead of throwing. normalizeReview inserts that invalid record at line 131, so callers cannot distinguish malformed review output from a real finding.

findings.title: Preserve normalizeReview's lenient-mode compatibility
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported optional strict parameter was removed. Existing callers using normalizeReview(raw, false) previously caught and filtered malformed findings; this version ignores the argument and maps directly. A null finding now throws at line 96, while an object such as {} is emitted as a bogus finding.

findings.title: Keep rejecting malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid input such as a bogus severity, empty required fields, or lineStart 0 now produces a Finding with P1/bug/empty/zero fallbacks instead of raising. Callers cannot distinguish malformed review data from a real finding.

findings.title: Preserve the public strict review mode
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview(raw, false) previously filtered malformed findings, but the second parameter is removed and every entry is now mapped unconditionally. TypeScript callers passing the existing argument no longer compile, while runtime callers receive changed results.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating valid-looking ones
findings.whyItBreaks: Input such as {"severity":"BOGUS"} now produces severity P1, category bug, empty required strings, and lineStart/lineEnd 0 instead of raising. normalizeReview includes that record as a real finding, so malformed output is indistinguishable from a legitimate finding.

findings.title: Keep the explicit repository for manual PR ref lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: workflow_dispatch leaves EVENT_HEAD empty, so these commands run before checkout without -R/--repo or GH_REPO. On a clean runner, gh cannot determine the repository, so the requested PR SHAs are not produced and checkout/review cannot target the selected PR.

findings.title: Keep the repository explicit for manual PR lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, these commands run before actions/checkout and the workspace has no repository context. Without -R "$REPO" or GH_REPO, gh pr view cannot resolve the repository, so the refs step fails and the review never starts.

findings.title: Preserve the repository when resolving manually dispatched PR refs
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so these commands run before actions/checkout. Without -R or an equivalent repository setting, gh pr view cannot infer the repository from the workspace and exits before producing the refs needed by checkout and the review.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-review errors instead of returning an empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed checks previously threw for null, non-object, missing, or wrongly typed review fields. The new code converts those failures into a valid-looking RawReview with empty/default values, so malformed upstream output can be treated as a clean review with no findings.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-review errors
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview previously threw when the input or any required field was malformed. The new code defaults missing or invalid fields to empty values, making malformed output indistinguishable from a legitimate empty review and allowing failures to be treated as valid results.

findings.title: Reject malformed reviews instead of defaulting them
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, invalid input or missing required fields threw an error. Now normalizeReview({}) or normalizeReview(null) returns an empty RawReview, making malformed output indistinguishable from a legitimate review with no findings.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for manual reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: workflow_dispatch provides pr_number but no pull_request payload, so this expression selects github.ref rather than the requested PR head. Lines 35 and 45-46 also default the base branch to main and pass empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA, causing the review command at line 47 to inspect the wrong checkout or lack its requested SHAs.

findings.title: Preserve PR ref resolution for manual dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: workflow_dispatch has no pull_request payload, so checkout falls back to github.ref instead of the requested PR head. The base fallback is hardcoded to main, while this repository uses master, so the fetch can fail; PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA are also empty on lines 45-46.

findings.title: Resolve the selected PR refs before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: workflow_dispatch events have no pull_request payload, so this falls back to github.ref—the branch or tag selected for dispatch—instead of the PR named by pr_number. The later PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA values are also empty, and the base fetch defaults to main, allowing manual reviews to execute the wrong reviewer version and compare the wrong commits.

findings.title: Restore the git output buffer for large reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync now uses Node's 1 MiB default maxBuffer. The full git diff collected at line 100 exceeds that for large PRs, causing git() to throw before review() runs; the previous implementation allowed up to 64 MiB.

findings.title: Restore the large buffer for local git output
findings.whyItBreaks: Omitting maxBuffer makes spawnSync terminate git when git diff emits more than Node's roughly 1 MiB default. The resulting ENOBUFS has status null, so runLocal throws at the git diff call instead of reviewing large patches; the previous code supported up to 64 MiB.

findings.title: Keep the 64 MiB buffer for git output
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync now uses Node's 1 MiB default maxBuffer. The git diff captured at src/adapters/local.ts:100 can commonly exceed that size; spawnSync then aborts and runLocal throws before review instead of handling the complete patch.

findings.title: Bind the PR diff lookup to the target repository
findings.whyItBreaks: ghText invokes `gh pr diff` without the supplied cwd or a `--repo` argument. When runGithub is invoked from outside cwd or another checkout, gh resolves the PR number against the process repository or fails, causing the wrong diff to be reviewed or aborting before the error check is posted.

findings.title: Keep review execution errors as failing checks
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch path still reports that the review did not pass and sets process.exitCode to 1, but the GitHub check-run conclusion is now `neutral` instead of `failure`. Check consumers that rely on the conclusion receive a downgraded non-failure result for an execution error.

findings.title: Derive changed files from the same PR revision
findings.whyItBreaks: The bundle patch now comes from the live PR, while changedFileSet still computes `git diff baseSha HEAD` against the local checkout. On a base-branch or stale checkout, the patch contains PR changes but changedPaths does not; the inline-comment filter then silently omits comments for actual changed files.

findings.title: Keep review failures as failing check conclusions
findings.whyItBreaks: The error path previously posted conclusion=failure, but now posts neutral. GitHub check consumers can therefore handle an errored review as non-failing even though the process exits with code 1.

findings.title: Bind the PR diff lookup to the requested repository
findings.whyItBreaks: ghText runs gh pr diff without a cwd or --repo argument, so gh resolves the PR number from the Node process's current directory rather than GITHUB_REPOSITORY or the supplied cwd. From another directory or checkout, it fetches the wrong PR or fails before the review error handler runs.

findings.title: Keep the patch and changed-file metadata on one PR revision
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch is now fetched from the remote PR, but changedFileSet still diffs baseSha against the local HEAD. If Actions checked out a base or merge ref instead of the PR head, changedPaths can omit files in the actual patch, causing inline findings to be dropped and surfaces to be misclassified.

findings.title: Keep review failures as a failing check
findings.whyItBreaks: The error path now publishes the Needlefish check as neutral instead of failure. GitHub treats neutral as successful for required checks, so a review or posting error can leave the PR without a review while still allowing it to merge. See [GitHub's required-check documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/how-tos/merge-and-close-pull-requests/troubleshooting-required-status-checks).

findings.title: Scope `gh pr diff` to the requested repository
findings.whyItBreaks: `runGithub` accepts an explicit `cwd` and obtains the target repository from `GITHUB_REPOSITORY`, but `ghText` runs `gh pr diff` in the ambient process directory without `--repo`. When invoked outside that checkout, GitHub CLI can fail to resolve the repository or resolve the same PR number in a different repository, aborting or reviewing the wrong diff. The [gh pr diff manual](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_pr_diff) provides `--repo` for this case.

findings.title: Keep the diff and posted SHA on one immutable revision
findings.whyItBreaks: `headSha` is captured from the first PR API response, while `gh pr diff` fetches the PR's current mutable diff in a separate request. If the PR is updated between those calls, `review` receives the new patch but comments and the check are posted against the old SHA, producing stale or rejected review results.

findings.title: Keep the reviewer executable in the trusted checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR head is now checked out as the workspace and its src/cli.ts is executed directly. A PR can therefore replace the reviewer, forge a passing review, or run arbitrary code on the self-hosted runner with GH_TOKEN, which has pull-requests: write and checks: write permissions.

The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Run the reviewer from a trusted checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR head is checked out into the workspace at line 46, and this line executes src/cli.ts from that checkout. A same-repository PR can replace the reviewer to suppress its own findings or use GH_TOKEN, which has pull-requests: write and checks: write, while running on the self-hosted runner.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.

findings.title: Run the reviewer from a trusted checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR head is now checked out as the workspace and src/cli.ts is executed directly. A same-repository PR can modify that file or package lifecycle scripts, then run with GH_TOKEN, pull-requests: write, checks: write, and access to the self-hosted runner. This lets the PR control its own review and execute arbitrary code.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.

findings.title: Restore canonical severity parsing before validation
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation trimmed and uppercased runtime input, so values such as " p2 " became P2. The new exact-match check rejects them and returns P3, silently downgrading valid findings; normalizeReview maps external findings through this function at line 132.

findings.title: Restore severity canonicalization before validating
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation trimmed and uppercased severity values. Now inputs such as " p1 " fail exact membership and are returned as P3, so normalizeReview can surface a high-priority finding as low priority.

findings.title: Preserve severity normalization when changing the fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation trimmed and uppercased raw.severity, so values such as " p1 " became P1. The new exact membership check rejects those previously accepted inputs and returns P3, misclassifying the finding. normalizeReview maps every finding through this function.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex child process
findings.whyItBreaks: Omitting env makes spawnSync inherit process.env, exposing GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN to the Codex process and any commands it runs while inspecting untrusted PR content.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit env, spawnSync inherits the parent environment, including GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN. The Codex process and its subprocesses can now read these credentials while processing repository-controlled input; the base implementation explicitly scrubbed them.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Omitting env causes spawnSync to inherit process.env. Any GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, or GITHUB_API_TOKEN present in Needlefish is therefore exposed to codex and commands it launches; the removed filtering was the only credential boundary.

findings.title: Keep fork PRs off the self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the job-level fork check allows any pull_request, including forks, to run on self-hosted infrastructure. The workflow checks out the PR head, installs its dependencies, and executes src/cli.ts, giving attacker-controlled code access to the runner and the workflow token.

findings.title: Keep fork PRs off the self-hosted review runner
findings.whyItBreaks: Deleting the same-repository guard allows fork pull requests to reach a self-hosted runner, check out the attacker-controlled PR head, install its dependencies, and execute its src/cli.ts with GITHUB_TOKEN available. A malicious PR can therefore execute arbitrary code on trusted runner infrastructure and access runner credentials or state.

findings.title: Keep fork PRs off the self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the job-level fork guard schedules this self-hosted job for fork PRs. It checks out the fork's head SHA at line 23, then executes its installation and src/cli.ts code at lines 28 and 34, exposing the runner and GH_TOKEN to untrusted PR content.

findings.title: Keep zero-valued timeout overrides valid
findings.whyItBreaks: With NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0, the base code passed 0 to the hard-kill timer at line 124, while this change substitutes the 5,000 ms fallback and delays SIGKILL. NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 similarly changes from immediate give-up at line 123 to a 2,000 ms delay.

findings.title: Keep zero-valued runner delays valid
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 were preserved. They now fail the > 0 check and silently become 5000 and 2000 respectively, so timeout escalation waits longer than the configured no-grace/no-wait behavior.

findings.title: Preserve zero-valued runner timeout controls
findings.whyItBreaks: With value "0", the new > 0 check returns the 5000 ms or 2000 ms fallback instead of accepting zero. The consumers pass these values to setTimeout at lines 123-124, so existing users who configure immediate SIGKILL or give-up behavior now wait several extra seconds.

findings.title: Restore review coverage for files outside selected hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: Large reviews still cap the mapper output at six hotspots, but the removed tail hotspot no longer deep-reviews changed files omitted by the mapper or ranked seventh. Those files can contain bugs without reaching the critic or final verdict.

findings.title: Preserve deep-pass failures as blocking residual risks
findings.whyItBreaks: An exception from a deep review now escapes reviewLarge, so one failed runCodex or extractJson call rejects the entire review instead of returning a blocking residual risk and continuing to the critic.

findings.title: Forward deep-pass residual risks to the critic
findings.whyItBreaks: Deep responses can contain blocking residual_risks, but the aggregation now hard-codes residual_risks to an empty array. The critic therefore cannot distinguish an unresolved deep review from one with no residual risk and may produce a non-blocking verdict.

findings.title: Keep distinct findings from collapsing on title prefixes
findings.whyItBreaks: Findings with the same file, line, category, and first 60 title characters now share a key regardless of whyItBreaks. A distinct finding at the same location can be dropped before the critic, with only the higher-severity or first entry retained.

findings.title: Restore tail coverage for omitted changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: The mapped hotspots are capped at six, but the deleted tail-coverage block no longer adds changed files outside those six. If a seventh hotspot contains a changed file, the loop never deep-reviews it and the review can incorrectly pass.

findings.title: Forward deep-pass residual risks to the final critic
findings.whyItBreaks: Every deep response's residual_risks is replaced with an unconditional empty array. A blocks:true risk is therefore invisible to the critic, which can emit a non-blocking result and allow the final verdict to pass.

findings.title: Keep failed deep passes as blocking results
findings.whyItBreaks: A runCodex, extractJson, or normalizeReview failure now escapes the hotspot loop and rejects reviewLarge before the critic runs. The previous catch recorded blocks:true and continued, so one transient or malformed hotspot response now aborts the entire large-review workflow.

findings.title: Keep base and head SHAs in both critic prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: The final critic no longer receives baseSha or headSha. In the large path it receives only patchStat, so it lacks the revision identifiers needed to inspect the exact base-to-head diff and validate candidate findings; the same context is also removed from the small-path critic.

findings.title: Retain failure reasons in finding deduplication
findings.whyItBreaks: Findings from separate hotspot passes now collide whenever file, lineStart, category, and the first 60 title characters match, regardless of whyItBreaks. One distinct finding is silently discarded before the final critic; the previous key retained the first 80 normalized reason characters.

findings.title: Keep one failed hotspot from aborting the entire large review
findings.whyItBreaks: A runCodex or extractJson failure now escapes reviewLarge. The previous handler recorded a blocking residual and continued, so review() now rejects without returning any review result when one hotspot fails.

findings.title: Forward deep-pass residual risks to the critic
findings.whyItBreaks: A deep pass can return a blocking residual risk, but candidateMerged now always supplies residual_risks: []. The critic therefore cannot preserve known unresolved review gaps, allowing the final result to omit a required block.

findings.title: Restore coverage for changed files outside selected hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: For a large bundle, the mapper can return hotspots that do not cover every changed file. After selecting only six hotspots, the loop reviews only those files; with the coverage backstop removed, omitted files are silently never deep-reviewed.

findings.title: Keep distinct failure reasons in the deduplication key
findings.whyItBreaks: Findings from different hotspots with the same file, line, category, and first 60 normalized title characters but different whyItBreaks text now share a key, so dedup keeps only one independently actionable defect.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's focus in large-patch reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: The large-review deep prompt no longer replaces {{FOCUS}}, so a non-null Bundle.focus is omitted from every hotspot review, while the small-review path still passes the full bundle.

findings.title: Preserve focus when building large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: When a large bundle enters reviewLarge, each deep prompt no longer interpolates bundle.focus, so focused review requests are ignored for every hotspot. The mapper also no longer receives focus.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into the minute count
findings.whyItBreaks: For 119500 ms, the code computes minutes=1 and seconds=60, so renderMarkdown emits `1m 60s` instead of `2m 0s`. The same issue emits `60s` for 59500 ms.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into the minute count
findings.whyItBreaks: For 119500ms, minutes is 1 and rounded seconds is 60, producing "1m 60s" instead of the canonical "2m 0s". The same issue produces "60s" for 59500ms.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into the next minute
findings.whyItBreaks: Minutes are floored before the remainder is rounded. For 59999ms this computes minutes=0 and seconds=60, rendering "60s"; for 119999ms it renders "1m 60s" instead of "2m 0s". Both stats and total-duration output use this formatter.

findings.title: Reject zero in the positive-integer parser
findings.whyItBreaks: parsePositiveInteger("0", label) now returns 0 even though its public name and error contract promise a positive integer, so callers receive an invalid value instead of a validation error.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: With the new '< 0' check, input "0" passes validation and is returned, contradicting the exported function name and its 'positive integer' error contract. Callers can receive zero as a valid positive integer.

findings.title: Reject zero and empty input in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported parser promises a positive integer, but Number("0") and Number("") both produce 0, which the changed parsed < 0 guard accepts and returns instead of throwing.
